Chapter 6: Preventing Relapse and Navigating Triggers
After those first big steps in recovery, things start to shift. Now, it’s all about keeping the progress going—and making sure you don’t slip back into old habits. This stage isn’t about those dramatic, movie-moment breakthroughs. It’s more like steady, day-by-day resilience.
And you know what? If a relapse does happen, it doesn’t mean you’ve failed. Think of it like hiking a tough trail—sometimes you lose your way, but you can always get back on track.
The real challenge in this phase? Triggers. Those are the things—maybe a place, a feeling, or a situation—that suddenly make cravings or old routines pop up again. Sometimes it’s external, like walking by a spot where you used to use. Other times, it sneaks up from the inside—stress, loneliness, or just plain boredom. Spotting these triggers and knowing how to handle them is absolutely key for long-term recovery.
So, what actually helps prevent relapse? Let’s break it down:
First, identifying your personal triggers. A lot of people find it helpful to keep a journal or just reflect on what situations really test them. When you know what sets you off, you can prepare.
Next, it’s about developing coping strategies. Maybe it’s taking a few deep breaths, texting a friend, or doing something that distracts you—like listening to music or going for a walk. These techniques can really help you ride out those tough moments.
Then, there’s creating a safety plan. Imagine you suddenly get hit with a craving—what’s your move? Having a simple, step-by-step plan, like leaving the room or calling your sponsor, can be a lifesaver.
And don’t forget about building new routines. When you fill your time with healthier, more meaningful activities, there’s just less space for old habits to sneak back in.
Let’s make this real: picture someone who used to use opioids after work to unwind. In recovery, they might swap that out for a walk in the park, a chat with a friend, or trying out a creative hobby. Over time, those new routines become anchors—helping them get through rough patches without falling back into old patterns.
The truth is, relapse prevention isn’t about being perfect. It’s about building awareness, treating yourself with kindness, and learning from any setbacks. Every single time you face a trigger and choose not to use, you’re bolstering your confidence—and your resilience—step by step.
